idiom_name: std::optional<T> for the 0..1 focus; index or range-for loop for 0..n
implementation_notes: std::optional<T> is the absence-carrying 0..1 focus (C++17) and a plain loop or range-for over the container is the plural traversal; the update function is applied to each dereferenced element, so structure and order are preserved. This is the widest-applicable realization and therefore the default. The classic optic structure (a first-class composable accessor) is replaced by these two standard-library mechanisms; reach for ranges or a library only when the same path is composed in several places.
pitfalls: Before C++23 there are no monadic operations on std::optional: chaining several maybe-absent steps means nested ifs, an and_then from another library, or a C++23 floor.
std::optional<bool> or std::optional<int> blurs the difference between no value and a value that is false/0; test with has_value()/explicit bool and use value_or for defaults.
A range-for mutates through the reference only when the element is taken by reference; iterating by value copies the optional and the update is lost.

variants.name: std::ranges filter/transform pipeline (C++20)
variants.implementation_notes: The C++20 range adaptors express the plural traversal declaratively: filter drops absent or non-matching elements and transform maps the remaining ones, and the pipeline composes and stays lazy. Use it when the traversal is over a range and reads better as a data-flow expression; the 0..1 focus still belongs to std::optional, because ranges traverse 0..n and cannot represent at most one.
pitfalls: A filter_view holds iterators into its source range, so a view over a temporary dangles; keep the underlying container alive for the whole pipeline.
Views are lazy and a pipeline that is never consumed does nothing, so an update written as a pipeline silently no-ops if the loop is dropped.

variants.name: std::optional monadic operations (C++23)
variants.implementation_notes: C++23 adds monadic operations so a chain of maybe-absent steps reads as a pipeline: transform maps the contained value (map in other languages), and_then chains a step that itself returns std::optional (flatMap), and or_else supplies a fallback. This is the closest direct standard-library realization of the 0..1 optional optic; it covers a single focus only, so a plural focus still needs ranges or a loop.
variants.code_sketch:
std::optional<int> port =
    config.get("server")
          .and_then([](const Server& s) { return s.port(); })   // flatMap
          .transform([](int p) { return p + 1000; });           // map
pitfalls: and_then requires the callable to return std::optional while transform does not; a mismatch is ill-formed rather than a diagnostic about the chain.
Monadic operations are guarded by the feature-test macro __cpp_lib_optional (202110L); without the check the code simply fails to compile on older standard libraries.
